title: CLO 2026 Academic Month: Sharing Multidimensional Breakthrough Methods for Talent Development in Intelligent Apparel
description: CLO 2026 Official Academic Monthly Course Review Released! Zhang Yujie, a full-time lecturer at Jiaxing Vocational and Technical College, shares online about the digital intelligence talent training program and practical achievements.
transcript:
Hello everyone, I am Zhang Yu-jie, a lecturer in fashion and clothing design at Jiaxin Professional Academy of Technology.  
I am very honored to be on the Cloud2026 digital fashion academic platform,  
and to have the opportunity to discuss and communicate with friends concerned about digital fashion and clothing talent training across the country.  
Today, I would like to share the topic of digital clothing talent training as a breakthrough approach.  

In recent years, the entire clothing industry has undergone profound reform.  
From traditional paper patterns and tailoring to fabric, digital and virtual fashion, and now to AIGC and 3D co-creation,  
digitalization and intelligentization are no longer optional but essential to our clothing industry.  

Therefore, our school, as a professional institution, is gradually restructuring courses and talent training systems.  
Here are some of my personal introductions and awards.  
In recent years, I have been fortunate to participate and achieve results in various 3D competitions.  
As a frontline professional education teacher,  
my core idea now is to focus on cultivating the real needs of enterprises,  
those talents who can be retained and utilized effectively, and to develop quality digital clothing professionals.  

Combining my years of digital teaching experience, business project experience,  
and guiding students in competitions,  
I will begin my sharing with the following five points.  

First, the first part is to create a timely plan for training digital clothing talents.  
In this part, the first problem we must solve is what to teach,  
and how to teach it so that it accurately matches enterprise needs.  
Therefore, grasping core competencies and customizing abilities according to enterprise requirements are very important.  

In deep cooperation with enterprises,  
what I hear most is that digital transformation in clothing enterprises is difficult, costly, and time-consuming,  
especially for frontline employees.  
They usually work very hard,  
and it is difficult for them to learn 3D digital skills systematically.  
However, they can accept small, step-by-step learning.  
Thus, what they lack most now are comprehensive digital talents who can be deployed immediately.  

When connecting with enterprise classes,  
I clarify a knowledge map with the enterprises regarding the skills students need.  
On the right side is a knowledge map I created.  
It includes hard skills such as digital modeling, garment sample adjustments,  
sample rendering as mentioned by experts,  
and fabric production techniques—these are all hard skills.  

What about soft skills?  
For example, reporting skills, organizational and coordination abilities,  
communication skills, and endurance.  
By discussing this skills map with enterprises,  
we can make adjustments.  
The knowledge structure in the course will change the flexibility of teaching.  
So, in this part, we proceed accordingly.  

At the same time, we invite enterprises to deeply participate in arranging and customizing our 3D courses and systems.  
For example, at the beginning of our collaborative classes,  
we meet with top clothing enterprises,  
inviting enterprise representatives, including Human Resources leaders,  
to participate in customizing our talent training.  

For example, on the upper right side, there are 10 courses in the Asian class.  
Among them, 3D accounts for 5% conceptually.  
Students only need to understand what 3D entails.  
For example, the silk class requires more 3D modeling content  
because it has external 3D business.  
So, one class has 5% and the other 14%.  
The difference in the number of classes is about 100.  
Therefore, for enterprises requiring higher modeling abilities from students,  
we appropriately adjust the curriculum.  

Simply put, what does the enterprise need?  
We focus on what we need to teach.  
What does the position require?  
We focus on what to add.  

The second part is to participate in enterprise projects  
and gain real project experience  
by introducing enterprise projects so that students grow in the real world.  

I have always believed that  
it is better to let students do a real project  
than to say something 10,000 times in class.  
Experiencing actual combat difficulties stimulates their learning motivation.  

For example, we have long-term deep cooperation with local Longtou enterprises in Jiaxing.  
In teaching, we have integrated real orders, public service requirements,  
and regulations directly into our classes.  

Here is a real case from an enterprise with certain difficulties.  
Their public service details involve many elements,  
such as collars, waist belts, private lines, invisible square buckles, pins, waist buckles, and so on.  
These structures are relatively complex.  
There is also a backpack that can be paired with it.  
On the front, there is a three-dimensional cover.  
You can see this is a 3D cover.  
Among the samples given by the enterprises,  
the cover is actually incomplete.  
Our students need to add some independent samples through their own operations.  

At the same time, the enterprise’s requirements for fabric texture must be highly restored.  
So, when students think they are not doing practice questions,  
but completing a product the enterprise truly wants to deliver,  
they strictly follow enterprise standards to complete the whole process.  

This model brings three obvious changes:  
First, students’ learning motivation is stronger.  
Knowing their skills can directly generate income and be applied in the workplace makes them very happy.  
Second, their ability rapidly improves.  
They learn to analyze the structure of sample plates,  
and to match sample plates to each part.  
Upon graduation, they can connect directly to real enterprise projects.  
They can also adapt to workplace rhythms in advance,  
cultivating rigorous, detailed, and efficient work habits.  

At the same time, for enterprises,  
when we introduce real projects into classes,  
they can see students’ actual performance in battle,  
forming a dual feedback loop.  

The third part is that we have established  
a model of listening, feedback, and optimization—a dynamic teaching model.  
Teaching is not a one-way output.  
We aim to build a two-way feedback teaching model covering both on-campus and online students.  

When facing on-campus students,  
we interact online.  
For example,  
we conduct questionnaires in our study hall,  
and analyze responses to collect students’ real learning feelings and pain points.  

For example, in this feedback,  
we find many high-level difficulties such as wearability issues,  
details like belt covers and pockets,  
which students find very difficult.  
There are also issues like walking show models, simulation animations that are not smooth,  
which trouble them greatly.  

For these problems,  
I immediately adjust the focus of the next class,  
for example, how to improve student performance regarding wearability.  
We offer special practice sessions or strengthen skills,  
especially sewing line types—incorrect changes cause garments to differ from intended effects.  
Including adjustments to panel conflicts and walking show wearability problems.  

Through these trainings,  
we reduce teaching thresholds and gradually enable students to learn and apply skills,  
to master our overall 3D modeling process.  

Second, we connect 3D modelers who graduated from us  
to their enterprise projects.  
During teaching, we do not abandon these students after graduation;  
we continue to follow up with them.  

For example, some problems they encounter at work are addressed.  
For instance, a student may need to make adjustments in their position.  
As I mentioned, enterprises need talent flexibility.  
This student, for example, needs to take a break from 3D business and participate in other tasks,  
while still coordinating well in 3D business.  
Thus, the student communicates well with others in this process.  

In this process, if students have emotions or difficulties,  
we teach them accordingly.  
We also communicate with students online,  
bringing frontline position needs back to the classroom to update teaching content.  

For example, after entering the enterprise, this student not only needs to do 3D-related work,  
but also learn AIGC to communicate with other students.  
So, in this course, we integrate these skills,  
allowing students to keep pace with the frontline of our industry.  

The fourth part is that, as before,  
during training, many students easily get lost and feel unable to continue.  
They feel they lack the motivation to persist.  

Here, I want to say that projects drive students’ learning.  
For example, in 2024, I won a gold medal for the 3D digital restoration of traditional Chinese clothing.  
In the course, I share this experience,  
telling students the concept of the project and how I won the gold medal.  

For example, step by step,  
what we did first, what came next, and so on.  
I also share these materials with students elsewhere.  
Students watch my lecture and see that the teacher can win this award,  
which naturally boosts their confidence.  

During this project, you can see a five-stage South Tang fairy tale painting.  
The entire clothing decoration and layout are student-made.  
From early historical research, to human body production,  
to garment processing, fabric stickers, craftsmanship details, patterns,  
and final virtual display and rendering.  

In the entire complete project, students transform fragmented tasks into a full exhibition.  
You can see this exhibition corner at our school.  

Through such an exhibition,  
we also have a digital boy.  
Every year, there is a digital boy fashion show,  
so that our students’ designs can be seen and recognized.  

Next, I want to show you a B-team I brought.  
They completed the restoration of this Song dynasty listening soft painting.  
They also restored the decoration of our characters,  
the production of equipment,  
and the editing of accessories.  
This includes the efforts of the students.  

So, thank you very much to this platform for giving us this opportunity,  
so our students can also be seen.  
Please enjoy. Thank you.  

I wonder if it is possible to connect with a Japanese character in the middle.  
I found it interesting.  
I like the visual.  
I think I’d like to try it.  
It’s a good idea.  
I want to try it.  
I think it’s a good idea.  
I like it.  

The children have their own research, and through this research process,  
they gain a lot of improvement through practice.  
The whole project is designed and produced by them, including the presentation method behind it.  
I think they did this project with great care.  
In the end, the children can participate in the learning process.  

It has been a goal of the school to create an independent learning environment for students.  
When students have the above skills and experience,  
we seize opportunities to learn more, aided by these advanced skills.  

Thank you.  

We actively check our students’ results and guide them to participate in competitions.  
For example, I led them to participate in two Chinese traditional 3D clothing restoration innovative design competitions.  
The competition includes the entire industry, teachers, and students.  
In the second year, our students received an excellent award.  
In the third year, they won two bronze medals.  
Their progress has been remarkable.  

Additionally, we participated in a gold medal competition in 2025,  
a fashion digital design contest involving AIGC and 3D.  
They won a national gold medal.  

When students receive the award certificates,  
see their virtual work, and receive recognition,  
this confidence and motivation cannot be replaced by any classroom lecture.  

The fifth point I want to share is about multi-level standards,  
including enterprise and industry standards.  
Through lectures by business experts and special sessions,  
we help students better understand the digitalization requirements of clothing.  

At the same time, we connect all official-level tests and certifications,  
so students gain deeper understanding of industry and position standards and requirements,  
allowing them to transition from classroom to workplace.  

In terms of software operation,  
it’s not just about tool use or following processes step by step,  
but about learning to solve complex problems independently  
and complete design through the full process.  

From industry knowledge,  
to understanding the 3D logic behind clothing,  
to becoming a true designer, technical expert,  
and digital talent in the clothing industry.  

On the right side, we show students’ classroom cases transforming into business projects.  

So, everyone,  
our clothing digitalization channel,  
day-to-day business,  
technology is constantly updating,  
technology is constantly upgrading.  
Our original intention of talent training remains unchanged.  

In summary, the following four sentences:  
We should be talented in teaching,  
and not deviate from students’ practicality,  
and not deviate from enterprise needs in integrating production and education.  
At the same time, we should listen to feedback,  
and not deviate from industry changes.  
We should drive projects,  
and not deviate from practical growth.  

In the future, digital technology will deeply enrich the clothing industry.  
AI, 3D, virtual fashion, digital transformation  
will bring more possibilities.  

So I also look forward to working with you,  
teachers, industry partners, and colleagues,  
to contribute to the new power of our clothing industry,  
so that our ideas of art, innovation, and business  
can become reality from ideas.  

My sharing ends here.  
Thank you very much for listening.  
I also hope for more communication and guidance.  
Thank you.

chunks.title: CLO 2026 Academic Month: Sharing Multidimensional Breakthrough Methods for Talent Development in Intelligent Apparel
chunks.content: # Sharing Multidimensional Breakthrough Methods for Talent Development in Intelligent Apparel This document presents a detailed account of digital clothing talent training methods emphasizing digital transformation, enterprise collaboration, project-based learning, feedback-driven teaching, competition participation, and multi-level industry standards integration. It focuses on 3D modeling, AIGC (Artificial Intelligence Generated Content), virtual fashion, and the development of practical skills aligned with enterprise demands. --- ## 1. Training Digital Clothing Talents: Matching Enterprise Needs and Core Competencies This section outlines the foundational approach to designing a digital clothing talent training program that closely aligns with the specific needs of clothing enterprises, emphasizing core competencies and customized curricula. - The clothing industry is undergoing profound reform from traditional tailoring and paper patterns to digital, virtual fashion, AIGC, and 3D co-creation. Digitalization and intelligentization are essential. - Educational institutions must restructure courses and talent training systems to meet these changes. - The key challenge is determining *what to teach* and *how to teach* to correspond precisely with enterprise requirements. - Collaboration with enterprises reveals that digital transformation is difficult, costly, and time-consuming for frontline employees, who prefer small, incremental learning steps. - Enterprises emphasize the shortage of comprehensive digital talents who can be immediately deployed. - A collaboratively developed **knowledge map** identifies necessary hard skills (digital modeling, garment sample adjustment, sample rendering, fabric production techniques) and soft skills (reporting, organization, communication, endurance). - Enterprise representatives, including HR leaders, participate in customizing course content and training systems. - Example: Different courses have varying 3D content proportions based on enterprise needs (e.g., 3D modeling constitutes 5% in some classes and 14% in others like silk classes with external 3D business). - Curriculum adjustments are made according to position requirements and enterprise expectations to ensure relevancy and practical skill development. --- ## 2. Integrating Real Enterprise Projects for Practical Experience This section describes the use of real enterprise projects in training to enhance student motivation, skill acquisition, and workplace readiness. - Hands-on experience with real projects is prioritized over theoretical instruction. - Long-term cooperation with local enterprises (e.g., Longtou enterprises in Jiaxing) incorporates actual orders, public service requirements, and regulations into coursework. - Example project involves complex garment structures such as collars, waist belts, private lines, invisible square buckles, pins, and backpacks with 3D covers. - Students contribute by completing incomplete samples and restoring fabric texture with high fidelity, following strict enterprise standards. - Benefits of this model: - Increased learning motivation as students see their skills translate to workplace income and impact. - Accelerated skill development in structural analysis, sample plate matching, and adaptation to workplace rhythms. - Graduates can directly engage in enterprise projects with rigorous, detailed, and efficient work habits. - Enterprises gain insight into student performance, creating a dual feedback loop between education and industry. --- ## 3. Dynamic Teaching Model: Listening, Feedback, and Optimization This section explains a responsive teaching model incorporating student feedback and ongoing adjustment to improve skill acquisition and relevance.

chunks.content: - Accelerated skill development in structural analysis, sample plate matching, and adaptation to workplace rhythms. - Graduates can directly engage in enterprise projects with rigorous, detailed, and efficient work habits. - Enterprises gain insight into student performance, creating a dual feedback loop between education and industry. --- ## 3. Dynamic Teaching Model: Listening, Feedback, and Optimization This section explains a responsive teaching model incorporating student feedback and ongoing adjustment to improve skill acquisition and relevance. - Teaching is interactive and bidirectional, involving both on-campus and online students. - Tools such as questionnaires collect student feedback on learning difficulties, including wearability, garment details (belt covers, pockets), animation smoothness, and walking show simulations. - Feedback informs immediate curriculum adjustments and special practice sessions focusing on problematic areas like sewing line types, panel conflicts, and wearability challenges. - The teaching threshold is reduced gradually, enabling students to master the 3D modeling process. - Post-graduation follow-up supports alumni working in enterprises, helping solve work-related problems and maintaining skill relevance. - Students often need to balance 3D tasks with other roles, requiring communication and coordination skills. - The curriculum integrates emerging skills such as AIGC to keep pace with frontline industry developments. - This continuous feedback loop ensures teaching content evolves based on real workplace needs and student experiences. --- ## 4. Project-Driven Motivation and Competition Participation This section highlights how project achievements and competition success enhance student motivation, confidence, and practical skills. - Projects serve as key motivators, helping students persist through challenges. - Example: In 2024, Zhang Yu-jie won a gold medal for 3D digital restoration of traditional Chinese clothing, which is shared with students to inspire confidence. - Project stages include historical research, human body production, garment processing, fabric application, craftsmanship, pattern making, and virtual rendering. - The final project becomes a full exhibition displayed at the school, showcasing student work. - Annual digital boy fashion shows provide public recognition for student designs. - Another project involved restoring Song dynasty listening soft paintings, including character decoration and accessory production. - Students engage deeply in research, design, production, and presentation, fostering independent learning and practical experience. - Participation in competitions has yielded excellent awards and bronze medals in 3D clothing restoration and digital design contests, including a national gold medal in 2025 involving AIGC and 3D. - Recognition through awards and virtual work exhibitions builds confidence and motivation beyond classroom lectures. --- ## 5. Multi-Level Standards: Industry, Enterprise, and Certification Integration This section discusses the incorporation of multi-level standards and certifications to prepare students for seamless transition into the digital clothing industry. - Students receive lectures by business experts and special sessions focused on understanding digitalization requirements in apparel production. - The curriculum aligns with official industry tests and certifications to deepen students' understanding of standards. - Training emphasizes not only software proficiency and process adherence but also independent problem-solving and full-process design completion. - Students develop industry knowledge, 3D logic comprehension, and the ability to become designers, technical experts, and digital professionals.

chunks.title: CLO 2026 Academic Month: Sharing Multidimensional Breakthrough Methods for Talent Development in Intelligent Apparel
chunks.content: Multi-Level Standards: Industry, Enterprise, and Certification Integration This section discusses the incorporation of multi-level standards and certifications to prepare students for seamless transition into the digital clothing industry. - Students receive lectures by business experts and special sessions focused on understanding digitalization requirements in apparel production. - The curriculum aligns with official industry tests and certifications to deepen students' understanding of standards. - Training emphasizes not only software proficiency and process adherence but also independent problem-solving and full-process design completion. - Students develop industry knowledge, 3D logic comprehension, and the ability to become designers, technical experts, and digital professionals. - Classroom cases are linked to real business projects, reinforcing practical application and industry relevance. - The continuous upgrade of technology and business practices drives the need for talent training that stays aligned with enterprise realities. - The core principles of talent development include: - Maintaining practical relevance for students. - Aligning education closely with enterprise production needs. - Listening to feedback and adapting to industry changes. - Driving learning through projects and practical growth. --- ## Conclusion: Future Outlook and Collaboration Digital technology, including AI, 3D, virtual fashion, and digital transformation, will profoundly enrich the clothing industry. Collaboration among educators, industry partners, and colleagues is essential to translate ideas in art, innovation, and business into reality. The goal is to cultivate digital clothing talents equipped to meet evolving enterprise needs and contribute to the intelligent apparel industry's future. --- # Speaker Profile **Zhang Yu-jie** Lecturer in Fashion and Clothing Design, Jiaxin Professional Academy of Technology - Experienced in digital clothing education, enterprise collaboration, and student competition guidance. - Recipient of multiple awards in 3D digital restoration and fashion design competitions. - Advocate for project-driven learning and dynamic curriculum development aligned with enterprise demands.
